Chapter 7: The Weight of Loss — Grief, Healing, and Moving Forward
You know, no matter how skilled or dedicated the midwives were, loss was always part of their world. The East End had seen its share of heartache, but losing a mother or a child? That pain never got easier to bear. Every loss left its mark—a quiet ache that lingered long after the workday ended.
There was one winter that stands out. A midwife was called to help a family where a baby arrived too soon. The mother, already worn down by years of hardship, held onto hope as tightly as she could. The midwife did everything possible—every trick, every comfort she knew. But as the night wore on, the baby's cries faded. By morning, that tiny life had slipped away.
The family’s grief was raw, almost too much to witness. The midwife sat with them in silence, realizing there were no words that could truly ease what they were feeling.
Moments like this taught the midwives something important: there were limits to what they could do. They could offer comfort—a gentle touch, a listening ear—but sometimes, the outcome was beyond their power to change. The weight of those losses could make it hard to keep going. Some midwives leaned on faith, others found strength in each other, and a few found comfort in just knowing they’d done all they could.
The whole community had ways to cope, too. Neighbors would come by with food, share stories, or help out with the little things that needed doing every day. In this place, sorrow wasn’t something anyone had to carry alone. Instead, people shared it—lifting the burden together, one small kindness at a time.
Over the years, the midwives learned that healing wasn’t about forgetting. It was about finding ways to honor the lives they’d lost. Those memories stayed with them, shaping how they cared for others. The work was never easy, but it always meant something. And even in the face of loss, the midwives found strength in knowing that just being there—being present—really, truly mattered.
